title: Harvard Has Dropped Its SAT Requirement, But Don’t Expect More Diversity
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler responds to Harvard extending test-optional admissions by arguing that dropping the SAT will not deliver the diversity colleges hope for. She cites studies of test-optional colleges showing only a one-point rise in underrepresented students, because other criteria such as extracurriculars and recommendations favor the same privileged applicants. She traces the SAT's history, from Conant's aptitude-based effort to widen access to its present reality as a test of the general academic knowledge and vocabulary wealthier children absorb earlier. Her real target is K-12 instruction: elementary schools that teach comprehension skills rather than content, and teachers trained to favor inquiry over explicit teaching, compound existing privilege. She therefore proposes knowledge-building curricula, explicit writing instruction embedded in content, and admissions assessments tied to what students have actually been taught. The piece originally appeared on Forbes.com.
points: Test-optional policies have produced only about a one-percentage-point increase in Black, Latino, Native American and low-income enrollment, because other admissions criteria favor the same students.
The SAT reading section still rewards general academic vocabulary and background knowledge, so it measures what wealthier children pick up at home rather than innate aptitude.
Wexler locates the real equity problem in elementary skills-focused reading instruction and inquiry-heavy teaching, which widen knowledge gaps.
Her remedy is coherent, knowledge-building curriculum with explicit teaching, and for older students explicit writing instruction embedded in content.
She would replace the reading SAT with assessments tied to taught content, such as AP, IB or the abolished Subject Tests.
quotes: But a recent study of 99 private colleges that adopted test-optional policies between 2005 and 2016 found that the proportion of Black, Latino, and Native American students increased by only one percentage point. The same was true for students from low-income families.

But the SAT, which requires students to analyze complex texts on random topics and understand sophisticated vocabulary, has never assessed innate aptitude alone. To a large extent it actually tests the general academic knowledge that wealthier students are typically better able to acquire, beginning at home.

Instead, instruction during the elementary years focuses on comprehension “skills” like “finding the main idea” rather than content, partly in a futile effort to boost reading test scores. And teachers have long been trained to favor “inquiry” and hands-on projects over direct explanation.
Eliminating or de-emphasizing the SAT and ACT won’t solve the college diversity problem any more than throwing away a thermometer will cure a disease.

The good news is that an increasing number of elementary schools are adopting curricula that teach kids to decipher words and simultaneously build academic knowledge and vocabulary. If students continue to get a knowledge-building curriculum, it’s possible that by eleventh or twelfth grade they will all acquire enough general academic vocabulary to demonstrate their potential on a test like the SAT.

At those grade levels, the best bet is explicit writing instruction embedded in the content of the curriculum and beginning at the sentence level. That approach can help compensate for large gaps in students’ background knowledge, build and deepen their knowledge of new content, familiarize them with the complex structure and vocabulary of written language—and boost scores on tests grounded in course content, like AP or IB assessments.
I would do away with admissions tests like the reading portion of the SAT, at least for the foreseeable future, and focus instead on assessments tied to content students have actually been taught.
